title: The dead
hookLine: you can forgive someone who has died

cards: A phone still holds a voicemail from someone who has died. It's two years old, about nothing, a question about dinner. And underneath it sits an argument that was never settled, because there was supposed to be time.
Now there isn't. The person who could apologize is gone, and so is the person who could hear one. It's easy to assume the door has closed.
Some very old texts say otherwise. Today: the dead.

teach.b: First, a king who gets the news. In the second book of Samuel, King David's son Absalom has turned against him, raised an army and driven his father out of Jerusalem. In the battle that follows, Absalom is killed.
David doesn't celebrate a victory. He goes up to a room over the gate and weeps: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee."

A son who tried to take his father's throne, and the father's cry is his name, over and over. Whatever lay between them, David's love goes on speaking to his son after he is gone. Second, the other direction.
The Talmud records a teaching for someone who wronged a person who has since died.

They can't go and appease the person anymore, so they bring others to the grave and say there, aloud, that they wronged this person. The words are still worth saying, in a place, with witnesses. Third, forgiving the dead.
If an apology can be offered to the dead, forgiveness can be too.

teach.h: THEY DON'T NEED TO TAKE PART.
teach.b: The other person doesn't need to take part.
Forgiveness, as this whole block has been saying, happens in the one who forgives, and saying it aloud gives it a time and a place. Fourth, what it doesn't require: pretending they were someone else.
Absalom still rebelled. Forgiving the dead is releasing what you're still holding, not rewriting who they were.

how: The Talmud describes going to the grave of someone you wronged and saying aloud, before others, that you wronged them; some people visit graves to speak to those they've lost, sometimes to settle what was left unsaid.

o: forgiveness or an apology offered to someone who has died
the custom of never speaking ill of those now gone
a belief that it's too late once someone has died

games.q: you're King David. your son Absalom raised an army against you and drove you from Jerusalem. a messenger arrives: Absalom is dead. what do you do?
o: thank the messenger for the victory.
go up to the room over the gate and weep for him.
say nothing and return to the city.
games.why: David weeps and cries his son's name over and over: "would God I had died for thee."

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died, with whom something was left unsettled; if that's too heavy today, choose something small, or simply sit with their memory.

If you can, say quietly what you forgive them for, one sentence is enough, or move your lips without sound if you're not alone. Then sit with whatever comes, and if you pray, you can name them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: The dead. Forgiveness, or an apology, offered to someone who has died, spoken in a time and place, even though they can't answer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: it still counts. They can't answer, and the words still matter. Day nine hundred eighty-three, done.
